title: 15. System Design Case Studies: Design Netflix
summary: Design Netflix at the scale of ~260 M paid subscribers in 190+ countries: video streaming (15% of global internet traffic), personalized recommendations, a microservices architecture deployed across multiple AWS regions, and…
objectives: Step 3: Deep Dive — Data Model (10 min)
Step 4: Deep Dive — Key Algorithms & APIs (10 min)

sections.title: Step 1: Clarify Requirements (5 min)
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Design Netflix at the scale of ~260 M paid subscribers in 190+ countries: video streaming (15% of global internet traffic), personalized recommendations, a microservices architecture deployed across multiple AWS regions, and the **Open Connect** content-distribution network (Netflix's purpose-built global CDN). Focus on **adaptive bitrate streaming via Open Connect**, the **recommendation pipeline**, and **resilience via chaos engineering** (the Simian Army). ---

### Functional Requirements
- **Browse**: home page with personalized rows ("Trending Now", "Continue Watching", "Because you watched X").
- **Play**: stream a movie/show with adaptive bitrate (240p–4K HDR), subtitles, audio tracks (multi-language), and seek.
- **Resume**: remember play position across devices; "Continue Watching" row updates within seconds.
- **Recommendations**: per-user personalized rows, refreshed daily and updated in real time as the user watches.
- **Search**: by title, actor, genre, mood.
- **My List**: user can save titles to watch later.
- **Ratings / thumbs**: user thumbs-up/down informs recommendations.
- **Profiles**: up to 5 profiles per account, each with its own recommendations and watch history.
- **Downloads**: offline viewing on mobile (DRM-encrypted files).
- **Multi-device**: web, smart TV, iOS, Android, Chromecast, game consoles, set-top boxes.

### Non-Functional Requirements
- **Availability** 99.99% for streaming (Netflix's most critical SLA — outage = subscription churn).
- **Latency**: time-to-first-frame p99 < 2 s; seek p99 < 500 ms; home page load p99 < 1 s.
- **Scale**: 260 M subscribers, ~200 M hours streamed/day, ~15% of global downstream traffic at peak.
- **Throughput**: peak evening = ~1 Tbps egress per region; 7+ regions × 1 Tbps = 7+ Tbps globally.
- **Storage**: 100 k+ titles × avg 5 GB per variant × 6 variants = ~3 PB master library; replicated to ~1 000 Open Connect appliances globally.
- **Durability** 11 nines for the master library (S3 multi-region replication).
- **Personalization**: recommendations refreshed daily; "Continue Watching" updated within 5 s of pause.
- **DRM**: Widevine (Chrome/Android), FairPlay (Safari/iOS), PlayReady (Edge/Windows) — required for studio contracts.

### Back-of-Envelope Estimation
- **Concurrent streams at peak**: ~30 M concurrent streams globally (evenings). Each at 5 Mbps avg → 150 Tbps egress.
- **Storage per title**: 1 movie × 6 resolutions (240p, 360p, 480p, 720p, 1080p, 4K) × 3 codecs (H.264, HEVC, AV1) × 5 audio languages × subtitle tracks → ~30 files × 2 GB avg = 60 GB per title.
- **Master library**: 100 k titles × 60 GB = 6 PB. Replicated to ~1 000 OCAs (Open Connect Appliances) → 6 PB × 1 000 = 6 EB total (with popularity-based replication — not every title on every OCA).
- **Recommendations**: 260 M users × 40 rows × 40 titles = 400 M recommendations precomputed daily.
- **Bandwidth cost**: if served from AWS CloudFront ($0.085/GB), 150 Tbps × 3 600 s × $0.085/GB = ~$50 M/day = $18 B/year — completely unsustainable. Netflix built Open Connect to bring this to ~$0.005/GB (custom hardware at ISPs).

### Scope
- **In scope**: streaming via Open Connect, recommendations pipeline, microservices architecture, resilience (chaos engineering), multi-region active-active, scaling.
- **Out of scope**: content production (Netflix Studios), billing (separate system), studio contracts/DRM internals (mention Widevine/FairPlay/PlayReady but don't deep-dive), live streaming (covered in YouTube design).

sections.title: Step 2: High-Level Architecture (10 min)
sections.body:
### Components 1. **Global DNS + Anycast** (Route 53) — routes viewer to nearest Open Connect cache. 2. **Open Connect CDN (OCA)** — Netflix's purpose-built global CDN. ~1 000 appliance deployments inside ISP data centers worldwide. Each OCA is a custom 1U/2U server with 100+ TB of NVMe storage, serving 40+ Gbps of video. Serves 95%+ of all video bytes; only 5% goes back to AWS origin. 3. **Edge / API Gateway** (Zuul — Netflix's open-source gateway) — TLS, OAuth, rate limiting, request routing. Deployed in AWS. 4. **Microservices** (500+ services, each independently deployable): - **Customer service**: account, profiles, parental controls. - **Title service**: catalog metadata (title, cast, synopsis). - **Playback service**: generates the manifest (HLS/DASH playlist) with DRM tokens; checks entitlement (does user have a valid subscription?). - **Recommendation service**: per-user personalized rows. - **Search service**: title/actor search. - **My List service**: user's saved titles. - **Rating service**: thumbs-up/down. - **Resume service**: play position per profile. - **Billing service**: subscription management. 5. **Cassandra / EVCache** — distributed cache and key-value stores (EVCache is Netflix's memcached-derived cache). 6. **MySQL / Aurora** — for transactional data (accounts, billing). 7. **S3 + Glacier** — master video library (11-nines durability, multi-region replication). 8. **Kafka** — event bus for play events, ratings, telemetry. 9. **Flink / Spark** — stream processing for real-time recommendations and analytics. 10. **Redshift / Snowflake** — data warehouse for analytics and ML training. 11. **Cookbook / Spinnaker** — deployment pipeline (Netflix's open-source CD tool). 12. **Chaos engineering infrastructure** — Simian Army (Chaos Monkey, Latency Monkey, Conformity Monkey) for resilience testing. 13. **Cassandra / CockroachDB** — multi-region replicated metadata store. ### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart LR U([Viewer Device]) --> DNS[Route 53] DNS --> OCA[Open Connect Appliance
ISP-embedded CDN] OCA -->|HLS hit 95%| U OCA -->|miss 5%| ORIGIN[AWS Origin S3] U -->|API| GW[Zuul API Gateway] GW --> PB[Playback service] GW --> REC[Recommendation svc] GW --> TL[Title svc] GW --> SRCH[Search svc] GW --> RES[Resume svc] GW --> CUST[Customer svc] PB --> EV[(EVCache
manifest cache)] PB --> S3[(S3 master
video library)] PB --> DRM[DRM license svc
Widevine/FairPlay/PlayReady] REC --> REDIS[(Redis rec cache)] REC --> EMB[(FAISS
title embeddings)] REC --> SPK[Spark nightly
personalization] SPK --> DW[(Redshift
warehouse)] TL --> CASS[(Cassandra
catalog)] U -->|play events| K[(Kafka
events)] K --> FL[Flink streaming] FL --> CASS FL --> DW K --> SIM[Simian Army
chaos tests] ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +----------------------+ | Viewer Device | | (TV / Web / Mobile) | +---+--------------+---+ | | video | | API v v +-------+------+ +-----+----------+ | Open Connect | | Route 53 -> | | Appliance | | Zuul Gateway | | (ISP cache) | +-----+----------+ +---+------+---+ | 95% hit | | 5% miss +--> Playback svc ----+ | v +--> Recommendation | | +---+---+ +--> Title svc | | | AWS S3 | +--> Search svc | | | origin | +--> Resume svc | | +-------+ +--> Customer svc | | | v v +-------+ +--------+--------+ | HLS | <----- manifest ---------| EVCache | | .ts | | (manifest cache)| | segs | +-----------------+ +-------+ | +-------------+-------------+ | | +----v----+ +------v------+ | DRM | | Cassandra | | license | | (catalog) | | (Wide- | +-------------+ | vine/ | | Fair- | +-------+-------+ | Play) | | Spark nightly | +---------+ | personalization| +-------+-------+ | +------v------+ | Redshift DW | | (ML training)| +-------------+ Play events -> Kafka -> Flink -> Cassandra (resume) + Redshift (analytics) Chaos: Simian Army continuously kills instances in production ``` ### Request Flow Walkthrough 1. **Home page load**: Device `GET /api/v1/home` → Zuul gateway → recommendation service → fetches precomputed rows from EVCache (per-profile) → returns 40 rows × 40 titles. Each title has a poster URL (served from CDN). 2. **Play**: User clicks a title → `GET /api/v1/play/{title_id}?deviceProfile=...` → playback service → (a) checks entitlement (valid subscription? region allowed?), (b) generates HLS manifest with available bitrates/audio/subtitles for this device profile, (c) generates a DRM license URL (Widevine/FairPlay/PlayReady based on device), (d) selects the best OCA for the user's location. Returns manifest + DRM URL. 3. **Stream**: Device fetches the `master.m3u8` from the OCA → measures bandwidth → picks variant → fetches `.ts` segments. Adaptive bitrate player switches variants on the fly. 4. **DRM**: Device contacts the DRM license service → exchanges a challenge for a license key (per-session, time-limited) → decrypts segments as they play. 5. **Resume tracking**: Every 10 s, device posts a `playback-progress` event to Kafka → Flink updates the resume position in Cassandra → home page "Continue Watching" row updates within seconds. 6. **Recommendations refresh**: Nightly Spark job processes the previous day's watch history for all users → generates 40 personalized rows per user → stores in EVCache. Real-time updates: if a user starts a new show, Flink immediately adds it to "Continue Watching."

sections.title: Step 3: Deep Dive — Data Model (10 min)
sections.body:
### Tables / Schema

**Cassandra — `viewing_history` (per-profile watch history, write-heavy)**
```sql
CREATE TABLE viewing_history (
    profile_id    UUID,
    watched_at    TIMESTAMP,
    title_id      UUID,
    position_s    INT,                -- playback position
    duration_s    INT,
    completion    FLOAT,              -- 0.0 to 1.0
    device_type   TEXT,
    PRIMARY KEY (profile_id, watched_at)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (watched_at DESC);
```

**Cassandra — `resume_positions` (per-profile, per-title)**
```sql
CREATE TABLE resume_positions (
    profile_id    UUID,
    title_id      UUID,
    position_s    INT,
    updated_at    TIMESTAMP,
    PRIMARY KEY (profile_id, title_id)
);
```

**MySQL / Aurora — `accounts` and `profiles`**
```sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id    BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    email         VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE,
    plan          VARCHAR(20),         -- basic | standard | premium
    region        VARCHAR(5),
    billing_day   INT,
    created_at    TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE TABLE profiles (
    profile_id    BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id    BIGINT,
    name          VARCHAR(50),
    language      VARCHAR(5),
    kids_profile  BOOLEAN,
    avatar_url    TEXT
);
```

**Cassandra — `title_catalog` (movie/show metadata)**
```sql
CREATE TABLE title_catalog (
    title_id      UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    title         TEXT,
    synopsis      TEXT,
    cast          LIST<TEXT>,
    genres        SET<TEXT>,
    maturity      TEXT,                -- G | PG | PG-13 | R | TV-MA
    duration_s    INT,
    release_year  INT,
    poster_url    TEXT,
    manifest_url  TEXT,                -- HLS master.m3u8
    available_until TIMESTAMP,         -- studio licensing window
    audio_langs   SET<TEXT>,
    subtitle_langs SET<TEXT>
);
```

**EVCache — `rec_rows:{profile_id}` (precomputed recommendation rows)**
```
SET rec_rows:{profile_id}  [
  {"row": "Trending Now", "titles": [uuid1, uuid2, ...]},
  {"row": "Continue Watching", "titles": [...]},
  ...
]
TTL 24h (refreshed nightly)
```

**Redis — `title_emb:{title_id}` (vector embedding for recommendations)**
```
SET title_emb:{title_id}  [0.18, -0.32, 0.91, ...]   // 128-dim float32 vector
```

**S3 — video library structure**
```
s3://netflix-master/titles/{title_id}/
  ├── 240p_h264/playlist.m3u8 + seg_0001.ts ...
  ├── 360p_h264/...
  ├── 480p_h264/...
  ├── 720p_hevc/...
  ├── 1080p_hevc/...
  ├── 4k_hevc/...
  ├── 4k_av1/...
  ├── audio_en.mp4
  ├── audio_es.mp4
  ├── subtitles_en.vtt
  └── subtitles_es.vtt
```

### Indexes
- Cassandra `viewing_history`: PRIMARY KEY `(profile_id, watched_at DESC)` — supports "show me my recent history" efficiently.
- Cassandra `resume_positions`: PRIMARY KEY `(profile_id, title_id)` — direct lookup for "Continue Watching."
- MySQL `accounts`: unique index on `email`; index on `account_id` for joins.
- Elasticsearch: inverted index on title, cast, synopsis for search.
- FAISS: ANN index on title embeddings (128-dim) for recommendation candidate generation.

### Storage Choice
- **S3 + multi-region replication** for the master video library — 11-nines durability, lifecycle to Glacier for unpopular titles.
- **Cassandra** for viewing history, resume positions, catalog — write-heavy, multi-region replication (Netflix uses Cassandra with `NetworkTopologyStrategy`, RF=3 per region).
- **EVCache** (Netflix's memcached derivative) for hot caches — recommendation rows, manifests, sessions. Sub-ms reads.
- **MySQL / Aurora** for transactional data (accounts, billing) — small dataset, strong consistency required.
- **Redshift / Snowflake** for analytics warehouse — ML training, A/B test analysis.
- **Open Connect Appliances** for video distribution — custom NVMe storage at ISPs.

sections.title: Step 4: Deep Dive — Key Algorithms & APIs (10 min)
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Pick the best Open Connect Appliance for the user.
- Generate an HLS manifest with available bitrates for this device.
- Batch-generate 40 personalized rows per profile.
- Add the title to 'Continue Watching' immediately.
- Home page (personalized rows)
- Playback (returns manifest + DRM URL)
- Playback progress (sent every 10s)
- My List (add / remove)

**Defines:** `select_oca()`, `generate_manifest()`, `generate_recommendations_for_all_profiles()`, `on_play_event()`, `ABRPlayer`

### API Design
```
# Home page (personalized rows)
GET    /api/v1/home?profile_id={pid}
       -> 200 OK { rows: [{ name, titles: [...] }, ...] }

# Title details (modal)
GET    /api/v1/titles/{title_id}
       -> 200 OK { title, synopsis, cast, similar: [...] }

# Playback (returns manifest + DRM URL)
POST   /api/v1/play/{title_id}
       { profile_id, device_profile, bitrate_cap? }
       -> 200 OK { manifest_url, drm_license_url, oca_hostname, expires_in: 7200 }

# Playback progress (sent every 10s)
POST   /api/v1/playback/progress
       { title_id, profile_id, position_s, duration_s }

# Search
GET    /api/v1/search?q=stranger
       -> 200 OK { titles: [...] }

# My List (add / remove)
POST   /api/v1/mylist/{title_id}
DELETE /api/v1/mylist/{title_id}

# Rating (thumbs up/down)
POST   /api/v1/ratings/{title_id}
       { rating: up | down }
```

### Key Algorithms

#### (1) Open Connect appliance selection (geo + load-aware)

```python
import geohash, requests

def select_oca(user_ip: str, title_id: str) -> str:
    """Pick the best Open Connect Appliance for the user."""
    # 1. Geo-locate user (maxmind IP database, cached)
    user_geo = geolocate(user_ip)   # {lat, lon, isp, country}

    # 2. Find OCAs in the user's ISP first (free peering, lowest latency)
    isp_ocas = OCA_REGISTRY.get_ocas(isp=user_geo.isp)
    if not isp_ocas:
        # Fall back to OCAs in the user's region
        isp_ocas = OCA_REGISTRY.get_ocas(region=user_geo.country)

    # 3. Filter by content availability (does the OCA have this title cached?)
    available = [oca for oca in isp_ocas
                 if OCA_REGISTRY.has_title(oca.id, title_id)]
    if not available:
        # Title not cached on any nearby OCA -> use AWS origin (rare)
        return f"https://aws-origin.netflix.com/titles/{title_id}/playlist.m3u8"

    # 4. Pick the least-loaded OCA (CDN reports load every 30s)
    loads = {oca.id: OCA_REGISTRY.get_load(oca.id) for oca in available}
    best_oca = min(available, key=lambda o: loads[o.id])

    # 5. Construct URL
    return f"https://{best_oca.hostname}/titles/{title_id}/playlist.m3u8"
```

#### (2) Manifest generation (per-device, with DRM token)

```python
import jwt, time

def generate_manifest(title_id: str, profile_id: str, device_profile: dict):
    """Generate an HLS manifest with available bitrates for this device."""
    # 1. Check entitlement (valid subscription, region allowed, not kids-restricted)
    if not is_entitled(profile_id, title_id):
        raise NotEntitledError()

    # 2. Fetch title metadata from Cassandra (cached in EVCache)
    title = get_title(title_id)

    # 3. Filter variants by device profile (mobile = no 4K, smart TV = all)
    variants = filter_variants(title.variants, device_profile)

    # 4. Filter audio/subtitle tracks by user's preferred languages
    audio_tracks = [a for a in title.audio_langs if a in device_profile.languages]
    subtitle_tracks = [s for s in title.subtitle_langs if s in device_profile.languages]

    # 5. Generate DRM license token (per-session, 2-hour expiry)
    drm_token = jwt.encode({
        "profile_id": profile_id,
        "title_id": title_id,
        "exp": int(time.time()) + 7200,
        "drm_type": device_profile.drm_type,   # widevine | fairplay | playready
    }, DRM_SECRET, algorithm="HS256")

    # 6. Build the manifest URL (points to OCA)
    oca_url = select_oca(user_ip, title_id)
    manifest_url = f"{oca_url}/{title_id}/playlist.m3u8?token={drm_token}"

    # 7. Build DRM license URL (player will request this to get decryption key)
    drm_url = f"https://drm.netflix.com/license?token={drm_token}"

    return {
        "manifest_url": manifest_url,
        "drm_license_url": drm_url,
        "expires_in": 7200,
    }
```

#### (3) Recommendation row generation (nightly Spark + real-time updates)

```python
# Nightly Spark job (runs at 2 AM local per region)
def generate_recommendations_for_all_profiles():
    """Batch-generate 40 personalized rows per profile."""
    profiles = load_all_active_profiles()   # ~200M profiles
    for profile in profiles:
        # 1. Fetch viewing history (last 90 days)
        history = get_viewing_history(profile.id, days=90)

        # 2. Generate rows using multiple algorithms:
        rows = []
        rows.append(generate_continue_watching(profile.id, history))
        rows.append(generate_trending_now(profile.region))
        rows.append(generate_because_you_watched(history))
        rows.append(generate_top_picks_for_you(profile.id, history))
        rows.append(generate_new_releases(profile.region))
        rows.append(generate_similar_to_mylist(profile.id))
        # ... ~30 more row types

        # 3. Rank rows themselves (which row goes first?)
        rows = rank_rows(rows, profile)

        # 4. Cache in EVCache (24-hour TTL)
        evcache.set(f"rec_rows:{profile.id}", rows, ttl=86400)

# Real-time update (when user starts watching)
def on_play_event(profile_id: str, title_id: str):
    """Add the title to 'Continue Watching' immediately."""
    rows = evcache.get(f"rec_rows:{profile_id}")
    cw_row = next(r for r in rows if r.name == "Continue Watching")
    if title_id not in cw_row.titles:
        cw_row.titles.insert(0, title_id)   # add at front
        evcache.set(f"rec_rows:{profile_id}", rows, ttl=86400)
```

#### (4) Adaptive bitrate player (client-side ABR algorithm)

```python
class ABRPlayer:
    """Simplified adaptive bitrate player (Netflix uses a similar ML-based algorithm)."""

    def __init__(self, manifest_url):
        self.variants = fetch_manifest(manifest_url)  # [{bitrate, resolution, url}]
        self.current_variant = self.variants[0]       # start with lowest
        self.buffer_seconds = 0
        self.bandwidth_estimate = 1_000_000           # 1 Mbps initial

    def on_segment_downloaded(self, segment_size_bytes, download_time_s):
        """Update bandwidth estimate after each segment download."""
        observed_bw = segment_size_bytes * 8 / download_time_s   # bits/s
        # Exponential moving average for smoothing
        self.bandwidth_estimate = (0.7 * self.bandwidth_estimate +
                                    0.3 * observed_bw)
        self._maybe_switch_variant()

    def _maybe_switch_variant(self):
        """Switch to a higher/lower variant based on bandwidth."""
        # Pick the highest variant whose bitrate < 80% of measured bandwidth
        # (20% safety margin to avoid buffering)
        safe_bitrate = 0.8 * self.bandwidth_estimate
        best_variant = max(
            (v for v in self.variants if v.bitrate <= safe_bitrate),
            key=lambda v: v.bitrate,
            default=self.current_variant,
        )
        if best_variant.bitrate != self.current_variant.bitrate:
            self.current_variant = best_variant
            log(f"Switched to {best_variant.resolution} "
                f"(bw={self.bandwidth_estimate/1e6:.1f} Mbps)")

    def on_buffer_low(self):
        """Buffer dropped below threshold -> immediately switch to lowest variant."""
        self.current_variant = self.variants[0]
```

sections.title: Step 5: Scalability & Reliability (5 min)
sections.body:
### Scaling Challenges
- **150 Tbps peak egress**: only Open Connect can serve this — AWS CloudFront would cost ~$18 B/year. Solution: ~1 000 OCAs embedded in ISP data centers, serving 95%+ of bytes locally.
- **Multi-region active-active**: 260 M users across 190 countries. Solution: 3+ AWS regions (US-East, US-West, EU-West, EU-Central, AP-Southeast, AP-Northeast, SA-East), each independently serving its region. Cassandra `NetworkTopologyStrategy` replicates data per-region.
- **500+ microservices**: each independently deployable, with its own database. Solution: service-per-team ownership, Spinnaker deployment pipeline, EVCache for cross-service caching.
- **Catalog updates**: when Netflix adds a new title, it must propagate to ~1 000 OCAs globally. Solution: scheduled "fill" jobs that push popular titles to all OCAs before launch; less-popular titles are pulled on demand.
- **Recommendation freshness**: nightly batch is too slow for "Continue Watching." Solution: hybrid — nightly Spark for batch rows + Flink real-time updates for "Continue Watching" and "Recently Added."
- **DRM across devices**: Widevine (Chrome/Android), FairPlay (Safari/iOS), PlayReady (Edge/Windows). Solution: DRM abstraction layer in the playback service; per-device token generation.

### Caching Strategy
- **L1 — Open Connect CDN**: video segments. 95%+ hit ratio. TTL 30 days (titles are static).
- **L2 — AWS origin (S3)**: master video library. Used only on OCA cache miss (5%).
- **L3 — EVCache**: manifests (5-min TTL), recommendation rows (24-h TTL), sessions, profile data. Sub-ms reads.
- **L4 — Cassandra**: viewing history, resume positions, catalog. Multi-region replicated.
- **L5 — Redis**: title embeddings (in-process for FAISS).

### Failure Modes
| Failure | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| OCA hardware failure at an ISP | Viewers in that ISP get slow streams | Route to next-nearest OCA; Netflix remotely reboots or ships a replacement |
| AWS region outage | Half the world's Netflix breaks | Multi-region active-active; Route 53 fails over to healthy region |
| EVCache cluster failure | Slow API responses, home page timeouts | EVCache is itself highly available (multi-AZ, RF=3); fallback to Cassandra |
| DRM license service down | New plays fail to decrypt | Multi-AZ deployment; license tokens cached client-side for 2 h |
| Cassandra split-brain | Inconsistent viewing history | Quorum reads/writes; LWT for critical updates |
| Spinnaker deployment bad | New version breaks playback | Red/black deployment; auto-rollback on metric regression |
| Studio licensing window expires | Title disappears but is cached on OCAs | OCAs honor `available_until` from manifest; auto-evict |
| Thundering herd (Stranger Things S5 release) | Millions start streaming simultaneously | Pre-fill OCAs with the new title 24 h before launch; pre-warm EVCache |

### Chaos Engineering — The Simian Army
Netflix pioneered chaos engineering to test resilience in production. The "Simian Army" is a collection of monkeys that intentionally inject failures:
- **Chaos Monkey**: randomly kills production instances during business hours. Forces services to be resilient to instance loss (auto-scaling, retries).
- **Latency Monkey**: injects artificial network delays between services. Tests timeout and circuit-breaker behavior.
- **Conformity Monkey**: finds instances that don't conform to best practices (no auto-scaling group, no monitoring) and terminates them.
- **Security Monkey**: detects security violations (open S3 buckets, missing IAM roles).
- **Janitor Monkey**: cleans up unused resources (orphaned EBS volumes, old AMIs).
- **Doctor Monkey**: detects unhealthy instances (CPU spike, disk full) and removes them.

The result: Netflix survives full AWS region outages with < 5 min user-visible impact. Real-world: Netflix stayed up during the 2017 us-east-1 outage that took down many major services.

diagram.title: Step 5: Scalability & Reliability (5 min) — step by step

steps.label: Scaling Challenges
steps.narration: 150 Tbps peak egress: only Open Connect can serve this — AWS CloudFront would cost ~$18 B/year. Solution: ~1 000 OCAs embedded in ISP data centers, serving 95%+ of bytes locally.

steps.label: Caching Strategy
steps.narration: L1 — Open Connect CDN: video segments. 95%+ hit ratio.

steps.label: Chaos Engineering — The Simian Army
steps.narration: Netflix pioneered chaos engineering to test resilience in production. The "Simian Army" is a collection of monkeys that intentionally inject failures: - Chaos Monkey: randomly kills production instances during business hours.

quiz.question: Why did Netflix build Open Connect instead of using AWS CloudFront?
options: Netflix's deployment pipeline (Spinnaker, open-sourced) is a multi-stage process.
Three layers of resilience. (1) Multi-region active-active: Netflix runs in 3+ AWS regions (US-East, US-West, EU-West, EU-Central, AP regions).
Studio contracts require DRM — Netflix cannot stream without it.
Pure economics. Netflix streams ~150 Tbps at peak — ~15% of global internet traffic.
quiz.explanation: Pure economics. Netflix streams ~150 Tbps at peak — ~15% of global internet traffic. At AWS CloudFront's egress price (~$0.085/GB), that's $50 M/day = $18 B/year — more than Netflix's total revenue.

quiz.question: How does Netflix's recommendation system work at a high level?
options: Live sports is fundamentally different from VOD. (1) Real-time ingest: stadium cameras push RTMP/SRT to regional ingest endpoints.
Netflix's deployment pipeline (Spinnaker, open-sourced) is a multi-stage process.
Spinnaker's red/black deployment makes rollback nearly instant.
Netflix's recommender is a hybrid batch + real-time pipeline.
quiz.explanation: Netflix's recommender is a hybrid batch + real-time pipeline. Batch (nightly): a Spark job processes the previous day's viewing history for all 200 M+ profiles. For each profile, it generates ~40 personalized rows ("Trending Now", "Because You Watched X", "Top Picks", "New Releases", "Continue Watching", genre rows, etc.).

quiz.question: How does Netflix survive an AWS region outage with minimal impact?
options: Chaos engineering is the practice of intentionally injecting failures into production to test resilience.
Spinnaker's red/black deployment makes rollback nearly instant.
Netflix's deployment pipeline (Spinnaker, open-sourced) is a multi-stage process.
Three layers of resilience. (1) Multi-region active-active: Netflix runs in 3+ AWS regions (US-East, US-West, EU-West, EU-Central, AP regions).
quiz.explanation: Three layers of resilience. (1) Multi-region active-active: Netflix runs in 3+ AWS regions (US-East, US-West, EU-West, EU-Central, AP regions). Each region independently serves its users.

quiz.question: How does Netflix's chaos engineering (Simian Army) work, and why?
options: Three layers of resilience. (1) Multi-region active-active: Netflix runs in 3+ AWS regions (US-East, US-West, EU-West, EU-Central, AP regions).
Spinnaker's red/black deployment makes rollback nearly instant.
Netflix's deployment pipeline (Spinnaker, open-sourced) is a multi-stage process.
Chaos engineering is the practice of intentionally injecting failures into production to test resilience.
quiz.explanation: Chaos engineering is the practice of intentionally injecting failures into production to test resilience. Netflix's Simian Army is a collection of automated "monkeys" that run continuously. Chaos Monkey: randomly terminates production instances during business hours.

quiz.question: How does Netflix handle DRM (Digital Rights Management) across devices?
options: Multi-pronged. (1) TTL on old history: add a 2-year TTL on viewing_history rows.
Chaos engineering is the practice of intentionally injecting failures into production to test resilience.
Pre-fill OCAs: 24 h before launch, push the show's segments to all ~1 000 OCAs worldwide.
Studio contracts require DRM — Netflix cannot stream without it.
quiz.explanation: Studio contracts require DRM — Netflix cannot stream without it. Three DRM systems are in use, each for a device family. (1) Widevine (Google): Chrome, Android, Chromecast, Android TV.
